9-hkdq3-k.title: A road trip from Yokohama to Nagoya—is it worth staying in Izu for 2–3 nights?
9-hkdq3-k.description: Is it worth stopping in Izu on a road trip from Yokohama to Nagoya? We’ll introduce Mount Omuro, the Ito hot spring district, unique cafes and local shops, and accommodations where you can enjoy all that Izu has to offer. We’ll also compare one-night and two-night itineraries and share tips on how to make the most of your time in Izu during your trip.
9-hkdq3-k.content:
I’m planning a road trip from Yokohama to Nagoya and would like to know if it’s worth spending two or three nights in the Shizuoka area (such as Izu), and if there are any unique cafes or boutique shops I should check out.

If you’re taking a road trip from Yokohama to Nagoya, why not stop by Izu Kogen along the way?

If you’re planning to stop in Izu between Yokohama and Nagoya, the Ito and Izu Kogen areas are relatively easy to incorporate into your route.

You can enter the Izu Peninsula from the Mishima area via the Izu Jukan Expressway and continue directly toward the Ito and Izu Kogen areas.

In Ito, you’ll find Mt. Omuro—a popular scenic spot that epitomizes Izu—as well as Tokai-kan, which retains the atmosphere of a traditional hot spring town with its historic wooden architecture.

Furthermore, Izu Kogen offers unique cafes, local shops, and places to enjoy crafts, allowing you to experience Izu in ways that go beyond simply visiting tourist attractions.

Day 1 | Yokohama → Izu Kogen

First, head to Mt. Omuro, an iconic landmark of Izu!

Take the Mount Omuro hiking lift to the summit, where you can enjoy a 360-degree panoramic view stretching all the way to Mount Fuji and the Izu Islands.

And there’s a special treat just for travelers coming from Yokohama.

If the weather and visibility are good, you can even see the Yokohama Landmark Tower from Mt. Omuro.

One of the fun aspects of this trip is that you can actually enjoy the journey itself.

At the summit, you can walk around the crater rim while taking in the scenery, and at the base, you can try your hand at archery.

https://omuroyama.com/

There are many restaurants around Mt. Omuro, but from the perspective of **“unique cafes”—the theme of this trip**—I’d like to suggest “Shiraki” and “See The Forest Coffee Roastery & Cafe” as top picks.

“Shiraki” is a small café located at the foot of Mt. Omuro.

What makes this place interesting isn’t just the food.

Behind the café lies a concept centered on “White”—a space that embodies living in Izu while hunting, eating game meat, and running the shop as a married couple.

Rather than simply “trying local specialties” at a tourist spot,

it’s more about getting a glimpse into the mindset and worldview of the people who live there.

I think this is a place where you can enjoy that kind of experience.

Hours are from 11:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and reservations are not accepted.

Therefore, rather than treating it as a must-visit spot, we recommend considering it as a place to stop by if the shop’s operating days and hours align with your itinerary.

Also, you can get a sense of the shop’s atmosphere and background through its official website and social media, so be sure to check them out before you go.

https://www.instagram.com/shiroki328/

https://note.com/chic_kalmia8125

“See The Forest Coffee Roastery & Cafe” is a small coffee roastery and café nestled in the woods of Izu Kogen.

In addition to enjoying their house-roasted specialty coffee, you can also savor meals like banh mi and avocado toast, as well as homemade baked goods and pudding.

The appeal of this shop isn’t limited to just coffee. The interior is lined with books, miscellaneous goods, coffee equipment, and tableware, giving the impression that it’s a place to enjoy the unique atmosphere the shop has created—rather than simply “going to a café.”

The shop’s name, “See The Forest,” takes the phrase “See the forest” from the proverb “Don’t see the forest for the trees,” embodying the desire to create a place where visitors can make new discoveries and gain fresh insights.

It’s about a 10-minute drive from Mt. Omuro, so it’s a great spot to visit in combination with Mt. Omuro and Shiroki.

https://seetheforest.shop/

Mount Omuro

↓ About 5 minutes by car

Shiraki

↓ About a 10-minute drive

See The Forest

↓

Accommodations in Izu Kogen

For those who want to enjoy not just “cafes at famous tourist spots,” but also the atmosphere, design, coffee, and even the merchandise at local shops, this place fits the theme of this trip quite well.

When choosing where to stay after a day of sightseeing, it might be best to base your decision on your specific goals.

If you want to enjoy cuisine unique to Izu, try “Izu no Hana, a Culinary Inn.”
If you want to casually enjoy an Izu hot spring inn, try “Izu Kogen Hinodeya.”
If you want to make the inn itself the highlight of your Izu trip, try “Oyado Uchiyama.”

① Izu no Hana: A Culinary Inn

A secluded retreat for adults, recommended for those who “want to stay primarily for the cuisine.”

Surrounded by bamboo groves, this quiet inn features seven guest rooms, each with its own private open-air bath. From the guest rooms, you can enjoy views of the Izu Sea and Izu Oshima, and relax in a serene, modern-Japanese atmosphere.

As the name suggests, the inn places special emphasis on its cuisine. You can enjoy kaiseki cuisine made with seafood from the waters off Izu and seasonal ingredients in a private dining room.

Also, considering that you’ll likely want to explore the Ito hot spring town the next day, reservations must be made by the previous business day, but a free shuttle service is available from Izu-Kogen Station and Futo Station.
While you’ll need to coordinate the return shuttle time with the inn, this is a very welcome service.

Recommended for

  • Those who want to fully enjoy Izu’s seafood
  • Those who want to relax at a quiet inn
  • Those who want a private open-air bath in their room
  • Those who want a touch of luxury but prefer to avoid large-scale hotels

Izu no Hana: A Restaurant-Focused Inn – Official Website

② Izu Kogen · Hinodeya

A great option for those who want to enjoy an Izu hot spring inn in a more casual setting.

Located in Izu Kogen, this ryokan serves cuisine made with seasonal ingredients from Izu. Depending on the plan, dinner features kaiseki cuisine, and for breakfast, you can choose between Japanese and Western-style meals.

They also offer room-only stays, and there’s a 24-hour supermarket right in front of the inn, as well as a convenience store about a 2-minute walk away.

This inn is convenient not only for those who “want to have all their meals at the inn” but also for travelers exploring Izu Kogen by car.

Furthermore, considering a tour of the Ito hot spring district the next day, its location—a 7-minute walk from Izu-Kogen Station—makes it ideal for a trip where you can leave your car at the inn and explore the Ito hot spring district on foot.

Recommended for

  • Those who prefer a more casual stay than a high-end ryokan
  • Those who want to spend plenty of time sightseeing in Izu Kogen
  • Those who want to stay at a hot spring inn but also enjoy dining out
  • Those looking to keep travel costs down a bit

Izu Kogen Hinodeya Official Website

③ Oshuku Uchiyama

A unique inn designed for “those who want the inn itself to be the highlight of their Izu trip.”

Located at the foot of Mt. Omuro, this detached inn limits its guests to just six groups per day. All guest rooms are private and feature their own open-air hot spring baths. The main attraction is the chance to soak in the hot spring while gazing out at the ocean and enjoying a peaceful retreat.

The cuisine strongly reflects the essence of Izu, offering “Uchiyama-style kaiseki” that features seasonal ingredients from both the sea and the mountains, such as spiny lobster, red seabream, and seasonal seafood. Great care is taken with the tableware and presentation as well. Abalone in thick sauce is featured as a breakfast specialty.

If you plan to explore the Ito hot spring district the next day, note that the inn is about an 8-minute taxi ride from Izu-Kogen Station; there is no free shuttle service.

However, since staying at Ryokan Uchiyama is about “experiencing the inn itself,” we recommend the following itinerary for the second day: check out → drive to Ito → visit Tokai-kan and the hot spring district → then continue on toward Nagoya.

Recommended for:

  • Those who want to make the stay itself the purpose of their trip
  • Those who want to experience Japanese ryokan culture
  • Those who want to enjoy a private hot spring
  • Those who want to enjoy top-class cuisine that embodies the essence of Izu
  • Those who prioritize a “special experience” over budget

Uchiyama Inn Official Website

Day 2 | Izu Kogen → Tokai-kan

After a leisurely morning at the inn, we’ll head from Izu Kogen to downtown Ito.

One place you’ll want to stop by in Ito is “Sweet House Wakaba,” a long-established coffee shop founded in 1948.

Its specialty is handmade soft-serve ice cream, which has been served since 1959. You can also enjoy traditional Japanese sweets like anmitsu. Currently selected as one of Tabelog’s “Top 100 Cafés 2026,” it is one of Ito’s most iconic, long-established cafés.

Located in Chuo-cho, about a 7-minute walk from Ito Station, it’s a great spot to stop by while strolling through the city on your way from the station.

https://izufull.com/wakaba/

After enjoying some sweets, head along the Matsukawa River.

Your destination is Tōkaikan, a historic building that epitomizes Ito Onsen.

Tōkaikan is a three-story wooden hot spring inn built in Shōwa 3 (1928). It is currently preserved as a tourism and cultural facility by the City of Ito.The interior features hinoki cypress, Japanese cedar, and unique “odd-shaped wood,” and intricate designs—visible in the corridors, staircases, and entrances to guest rooms—still showcase the craftsmanship of the artisans.

On a stroll through the Ito Onsen district, you can get a sense of what Ito was like in the past—not just through the buildings, but also through the streetscape itself.

This is a chance to enjoy “what remains of this land” itself—something quite different from the unique cafes and shops you’ll find in Izu Kogen.

From here, you can choose your own pace for the trip

If you’re thinking of stopping by on your way from Yokohama to Nagoya, even one night in Izu is plenty of time to enjoy the area.

However, if—unlike this trip—you want to enjoy the atmosphere of Izu itself by visiting unique shops, strolling through the hot spring town, and relaxing at your inn, rather than just “seeing a few tourist spots along the way,” staying for two nights will make a significant difference in your overall travel experience.

For a one-night stay, make the most of “Izu Kogen + Ito.”

If you stay two nights, you can add another day to enjoy hot springs, dining, and shopping, and leave your car behind to take a leisurely stroll through the town.

If you’re rushing to Nagoya, stay one night. If you want to make Izu itself one of the main goals of your trip, stay two nights.

That approach seems just right for this route.

We recommend deciding on your length of stay based on your own travel pace.

If you’d like to ask a local for advice, we offer free consultations.

Please feel free to contact us!

rcbv95om5.title: The History of Mt. Omuro
rcbv95om5.description: Mount Omuro was formed approximately 4,000 years ago. From its 580-meter summit, visitors can enjoy breathtaking 360-degree views, visit the Asama Shrine—which enshrines the rare deity Iwanaga-hime—and experience the “Yamayaki,” a traditional event with a history spanning over 700 years. This article explores the volcanic history and local culture hidden within this symbol of Ito.
rcbv95om5.content:
Mount Omuro is a volcano formed by an eruption approximately 4,000 years ago.

It is a “scoria cone” formed by layers of volcanic ejecta, and its distinctive shape—resembling an upside-down bowl—is also the result of this volcanic activity.

It stands at an elevation of 580 meters.
At the summit is a crater approximately 1 kilometer in diameter, and visitors can now walk around its perimeter on the “O-hachi Meguri” trail.
On a clear day, you can enjoy a 360-degree panoramic view of Mount Fuji, the Izu Islands, and Sagami Bay.

In other words,

it’s now a symbol of Ito as a “scenic spot,” but it was originally a volcano formed about 4,000 years ago

, isn’t it?

There is an Asama Shrine at the summit

At the summit of Mt. Omuro stands the “**Mt. Omuro Sengen Shrine**.”

Here, deities known for ensuring safe childbirth and fostering romantic relationships are enshrined, and it remains a place where visitors can stop by while walking around the crater rim at the summit. The official
Ito City tourism website states that Konohanasakuya-hime and her sister, Iwanaga-hime-no-mikoto—who are enshrined at Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha—are enshrined here.

While most Asama Shrines typically enshrine the younger sister, Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, Omuroyama is unusual in that it enshrines her older sister, Iwanaga-hime-no-Mikoto, alone.

The “Mountain Burning” Festival Has Been Held for Over 700 Years

The most fascinating aspect of Mt. Omuro is the “Mt. Omuro Yama-yaki,” held every February.

This event has a history of over 700 years.

At first glance, burning the entire mountain may seem like a rather unusual event, but it was originally carried out for the purpose of preserving the mountain and maintaining grazing lands.When it began
approximately 700 years ago, it was part of daily agricultural and domestic life,
aimed at cultivating high-quality thatch used for thatched roofs, compost, and livestock feed. Today, it has become a spring tradition in Ito.

By burning the mountain’s grass once a year, new grass grows, preserving that distinctive **“Mount Omuro, resembling a green pudding”**.

In other words, the beautiful landscape we see today

not simply a landscape left to nature, but one that local people have carefully tended and maintained over a long period of time

.

p9b85d4fd.title: The History of Tokai-kan | A Walk Through a Showa-Era Wooden Ryokan in Ito Onsen
p9b85d4fd.description: "Tokai-kan" is a wooden ryokan that preserves the history of Ito Onsen to this day. As we trace its journey—from its founding in 1928 through the end of its operation as a ryokan to its rebirth as a cultural facility—we’ll introduce the highlights you’ll want to know about before your visit, including the wooden architecture that showcases master craftsmanship, the watchtower, and the historic streetscape along the Matsukawa River.We’ll also explain its connection to *Thermae Romae*.
p9b85d4fd.content:
Along the Matsukawa River, which flows through the center of Ito, stands a particularly eye-catching wooden building.

It is the Tōkaikan.

Although it is currently open to the public as the “Ito Onsen Tourism and Cultural Facility Tokai-kan,” it was originally a hot spring inn established in 1928 (Showa 3).
Built by Antaro Inaba, a lumber merchant, it operated as an inn for approximately 70 years.

From the outside, it is an impressive three-story wooden structure.

However, the appeal of Tokai-kan lies not only in the size of the building.

Once inside, you can see the intricate details crafted by the artisans of that era everywhere you look.

It’s as if Ito Onsen itself from that era has been preserved within the building.

If you walk around with that sense in mind, Tokai-kan begins to look a little different.

1928: The Birth of Tokai-kan

Tokai-kan was founded in 1928, just as the Showa era was beginning.

Since the founder, Antaro Inaba, was a lumber merchant, the building features high-quality wood and “unusual timber” that makes the most of its natural shape.

Even today, visitors can see pillars and beams with beautiful wood grain, as well as uniquely shaped pieces of wood, throughout the building. The city of Ito also highlights Tokai-kan as a building where one can appreciate the craftsmanship of the era in its “notable and unusual woods,” architectural fittings, and intricate details.

How to showcase the wood, and where and how to incorporate decorative elements—

The work of these artisans itself is what makes this building so captivating.

The Opening of the Ito Line Brought Major Changes to Tokai-kan

The opening of the Ito Line in 1938 (Showa 13) is a pivotal event in the history of Tokai-kan.

According to the City of Ito, the opening of the Ito Line shifted the clientele—which had previously consisted mainly of visitors seeking hot spring treatments—toward group tourists, and Tokai-kan expanded its facilities accordingly.

In other words, the Tokai-kan building itself reflects the changing demographics of visitors to Ito Onsen.

The inn did not expand simply because it wanted to build a more impressive structure.

Railroads changed the way people traveled, and the nature of hot spring trips evolved as well.

In response to these changes, Tokai-kan also evolved.

A Showcase of Artisans’ Craftsmanship Remains Within the Inn

As you walk through the inn, you’ll notice that the atmosphere varies slightly from room to room.

This is one of Tokai-kan’s major highlights.

It is said that renowned master carpenters of the time each took responsibility for a different floor during construction, and you can see distinct designs in each area.

For example, the decorative windows in the guest rooms.

The staircase handrails. The shoji screens in the study. The floor pillars. The transom panels.

And the wood used throughout the building.

While each element may seem like a small decorative detail on its own, together they create the unique atmosphere of Tokai-kan.

The 120-tatami-mat grand hall is particularly breathtaking.

It allows us to imagine that ryokans of that era were not only places for individual travelers but also venues where large numbers of people gathered.

In 1949, the “Watchtower” was built on the rooftop

When viewed from the outside, the “watchtower” atop the building is what catches the eye.

It was built in 1949 (Showa 24).

At that time, there were few tall buildings around Tokai-kan like there are today, and it is said that one could see Mount Amagi from the watchtower.

While it is now a distinctive feature that embodies the “essence of Tokai-kan,” it also serves as a clue to imagining what the town of Ito looked like back then.

As you walk along the Matsukawa River today,

it might be interesting to wonder,

It might be interesting to ponder this.

Surviving Disasters and Continuing as a Ryokan

has continued to operate as a ryokan, and has undergone repeated repairs and renovations to keep pace with the times.

In 1958 (Showa 33), it suffered extensive damage from the Kano River Typhoon.

Nevertheless, thanks to subsequent repairs and renovations, it continued to operate as a ryokan.

Counting from its founding in 1928, Tokai-kan operated as a hot spring inn in Ito for approximately 70 years.

Then, in 1997,

It brought its long history as a ryokan to a close. The building was subsequently donated to the City of Ito.

From a Ryokan to a Cultural Facility

This marks the beginning of another chapter in Tokai-kan’s history.

Just because it had fulfilled its role as a ryokan didn’t mean the building was demolished.

In 1999, it was designated as a cultural property of Ito City, and preservation and restoration work was subsequently carried out.

Then, on July 26, 2001,

“Ito Onsen Tourism and Cultural Facility: Tokai-kan”

.

In other words, the current Tokai-kan is

was established in 1928 as a
hot spring inn

expanded in 1938
to accommodate the increase in group tourists following the opening of the Ito Line

In
1949, the observation tower was built

1997
: Ceased operations as a ryokan

In 1999, it was designated as a
cultural property of Ito City

2001
: Reborn as a tourism and cultural facility

After this long journey, it has taken on its current form.

As you walk through Tōkaikan, the history of Ito Onsen comes to life

The charm of Tokai-kan cannot be fully explained simply by saying, “It’s a Showa-era retro building.”

Here,

the history of how this hot spring resort developed

the era when the railway brought an increasing number of travelers

the skills of the artisans who supported the ryokan

and the efforts of those who sought to preserve the building after it had served its original purpose

are all intertwined here.

So, as you walk through the inn, please don’t just take photos of the rooms—be sure to take a closer look at the intricate details of the wood as well.

The grain of the wood on the pillars.

The banisters on the stairs.

The shape of the windows.

The design of the shoji screens.

The carvings on the transoms.

As you look at each of these elements, you gradually come to realize that Tokai-kan is not merely an “old inn,” but a work of architecture that people of that era created with great time and effort.

And by preserving the building, we today can imagine what Ito Onsen was like in the early Showa period.

If you visit Tōkaikan, be sure to take a walk along the Matsukawa River

If you’re visiting Tokai-kan, I recommend taking the time to view the exterior from along the Matsukawa River, not just exploring the interior.

The landscape created by the Matsukawa River, Tokai-kan, and the surrounding historic buildings is one of the scenes that symbolizes present-day Ito Onsen.

In fact, in July 2026, the city of Ito designated this area as an “Important Scenic District.” It has positioned the landscape—where the Matsukawa River and
historic structures like Tokai-kan blend as one—as an iconic symbol of Ito Onsen.

Explore the interior of the building.
↓
Take a walk along the Matsukawa River.
↓ Take
another look at Tōkaikan from the outside.

If you walk in this order, it might look a little different than when you first saw it.

Tōkaikan, which served as a model for *Thermae Romae*

There’s another interesting story about Tōkaikan.

Tōkaikan is known as one of the models for “Ito Onsen Tōrinkan,” which appears in Volume 4 of Mari Yamazaki’s manga *Thermae Romae*.

If you visit the actual Tōkaikan and then reread the manga, you’ll be able to enjoy the experience even more by comparing the atmosphere of the building with the one in the story.

*Thermae Romae* is a story about Lucius, an ancient Roman bath designer, who time-travels to modern-day Japan’s public bathhouses and hot springs and is amazed by Japanese bathing culture.

An Ito hot spring inn appears in this manga that bridges the “baths” of ancient Rome and Japan.

With that in mind, it might be interesting to read the manga before visiting Tōkaikan.

m2dn4z8_v6.title: On the way from Hakone to Kyoto, is it possible to stop by the Mishima Skywalk?
m2dn4z8_v6.description: Can you enjoy the spectacular view of Mount Fuji at the Mishima Skywalk while traveling from Hakone to Kyoto? Here, we’ll introduce how to get there by bus from Motohakone Port, the estimated time needed for your visit, and a sample itinerary for traveling from Mishima Station to Kyoto via the Shinkansen.
m2dn4z8_v6.content:
I’d like to know if it’s feasible to take a detour to the Mishima Skywalk on the way from Hakone to Kyoto, enjoy the view of Mount Fuji, and then board the Shinkansen at Mishima Station.

It is possible to stop by the Mishima Skywalk on the day you travel from Hakone to Kyoto.

At Moto-Hakone Port, there is a bus stop for the “Mishima Station (via Mishima Skywalk)” route.

https://transfer-cloud.navitime.biz/tokaibus/courses/timetables?busstop=00471500&course-sequence=0007801126-1

After visiting the Mishima Skywalk, you can head to Mishima Station and take the Shinkansen from there toward Kyoto.

We recommend allowing about 80 minutes for your visit to the Mishima Skywalk (excluding activities).

The walk across the suspension bridge itself takes about 10 to 15 minutes one way.

Depending on your purpose, the recommended stay times are as follows:

  • Just crossing the suspension bridge to enjoy the view: 40–60 minutes
  • Suspension bridge + observation deck, photos, shops, etc.: 60–90 minutes
  • Enjoying meals and cafes: 90 minutes to 2 hours
  • Including activities like the zip slide: 2 hours or more

Business hours are typically 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
Since the purpose of this trip is to enjoy the view of Mount Fuji and to stop here while traveling from Hakone to Kyoto, we’ve estimated a stay of 80 minutes. If you plan to stop by the Mishima Skywalk on your way
from Hakone and then head to Kyoto from Mishima Station, working backward from that schedule, it’s best to arrive at the Mishima Skywalk around 9:00 a.m.

9:00–10:20: Mishima Skywalk

Around 10:20: Head toward Mishima Station

Around 11:00 AM: Arrive at Mishima Station

Then, take the Shinkansen to Kyoto

This allows you to complete the route: Hakone → Mishima Skywalk → Mishima Station → Kyoto.

See Japan’s tallest mountain from Japan’s longest suspension bridge. Be sure to enjoy this once-in-a-lifetime experience.
